paras: In Chapter 4 we distinguished what should be remembered. There are people, events, decisions, and records, and there are relationships between them.
Once these objects are defined, the graph begins to take shape.
But another problem appears. What happens when several people begin creating that memory together?
A person can record something freely when the memory is private. Shared memory is different.
beats.claim: A person writes a record. An assistant proposes one. An agent finds a connection. Someone brings memory in from elsewhere.

paras: Two people may record the same event differently. One calls it an event, another an episode, and a third leaves it as a record.
Relationships diverge the same way. One person records that a decision happened because of an event. Another expresses the relationship in the opposite direction.
Each record can look perfectly reasonable on its own.
But once they are connected, the reader and the AI interpret the same meaning differently. Shared memory cannot depend only on personal expression.
Ontology distinguishes the world we remember. It defines concepts, records, decisions, and the kinds of relationships that may exist.

But ontology alone is not enough. How should the same concept actually be recorded? How should relationship direction be expressed? At what granularity should a new node be created? What should happen when duplicate memories are found?
These questions require convention, the shared rules for recording.
Ontology is the language of memory. Convention is its grammar. That distinction is a large part of why a graph here is more than a database.

beats.h: Machines Have to Read It Too
paras: If only people worked together, the rules could be explained in a document and agreed upon over time.
Vinc also has to account for AI and agents reading and writing the graph directly. So the rules need to be machine-readable.
What counts as a concept in this graph? Which edges are allowed? Which areas may be generated automatically? What requires human review?
If a person has to explain these every time, the same knowledge drifts whenever the agent changes.
And the drift is silent: nothing announces that this agent read the rule differently from the last one.
beats.claim: GRAPH.md is closer to a machine-readable contract than to a manual.

beats.h: The Contract Is Not the Memory
paras: GRAPH.md does not replace the contents of the graph. The canonical source of memory remains the graph and the records connected to it.
What the contract explains is how that memory should be read, extended, and connected.

So it separates areas maintained by people from areas that can be generated from the current graph state. Human-defined rules stay the responsibility of people. Anything derivable from present state can be regenerated at will.
The distinction looks small and is not: human judgment and reproducible system state should not be mixed together in one file.

beats.h: Not Every Rule Has the Same Force
paras: Graph rules should not all be treated as equally strong.
Some are fixed by the system, such as schema and basic integrity constraints. Some are decided by the owner or operator of a particular graph. Others vary with topic or situation.
Schema-fixed, this-graph-decides, varies-by-topic.
This matters because an agent should not mistake every sentence for an instruction of identical force. A memory structure contains both requirements and choices.
Is the format valid? Are the required sections present? Are the generated-zone boundaries intact? Do the references exist?
A system can check all of that.
But other questions are different. Is this really a good concept? Are these two records really the same memory? Is this decision still valid?

Those are judgments about meaning and context, so Vinc separates verification from judgment. The system reports broken structure. AI proposes merges and new relationships. Semantic changes stay reviewable by people.
A checker that tried to answer them would be guessing, and a guess recorded as a check is worse than no check.
beats.claim: An agent may propose a memory. It should not decide that the memory is true.

paras: Chapter 3 argued that what we show AI conditions its answer, and Chapter 4 that the material should be structured memory. One more step follows.
For structured memory to preserve meaning over time, it needs a grammar for recording it.
If today's decision and another person's decision months later follow different conventions, the two cannot be used reliably in the same graph.
With shared conventions, memory accumulates. One record sits on another. One decision leads to another. Experiences from different people connect inside the same structure.
beats.claim: The same memory can be read by the same rules, and new memory added in the same shape.

paras: Rules like these can look as though they exist for machines.
But what they ultimately protect is human memory.
They keep meaning from changing arbitrarily when the person changes, the assistant changes, the agent changes, or simply when enough time passes.
So the rules are not coding style. They are social and technical agreements that let memory continue in the same structure regardless of whose hands it enters.
Which is why the grammar is written down and versioned rather than carried in whoever happens to be maintaining the graph this month.

beats.label: 5.close
paras: If we can distinguish memory, connect it, and hold it to a common grammar, one question is still open: where does that memory exist?
There is time. There is position. There is distance. And the meaning of a graph can change depending on how we look at that space.
